title: Ukrainian Vinegret Beet & Potato Salad
dek: Tender beets, potatoes, carrots and peas meet briny pickles and sauerkraut in a bright, make-ahead Ukrainian-style salad with clean, distinct dice instead of pink mush.
image_alt: Bowl of Ukrainian-style vinegret with diced beets, potatoes, carrots and green peas
ingredients: 1 1/2 pounds medium red beets, scrubbed and trimmed to 1 inch of stem
1 cup dill pickles, drained and cut into 3/8-inch dice
1 cup sauerkraut, squeezed dry and coarsely chopped
1/4 cup chopped fresh dill or flat-leaf parsley, plus more for serving
3 tablespoons unrefined sunflower oil or extra-virgin olive oil, divided
1 tablespoon pickle brine or apple cider vinegar
3/4 teaspoon fine sea salt, divided, plus more to taste

instructions.name: Cook the beets in their own pot
instructions.text: Place the whole beets in a 4-quart saucepan and cover with cool water by 1 inch. Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and cover partially. Cook for 40 to 60 minutes, until a paring knife slides into the center with little resistance. Check smaller beets at 35 minutes and remove them as they become tender. Drain, cool until safe to handle, then slip off the skins.

instructions.name: Cook the potatoes and carrots to separate endpoints
instructions.text: While the beets simmer, place the whole potatoes and carrots in a second saucepan and cover with cool water by 1 inch. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt and bring to a gentle boil. Remove the carrots after 15 to 20 minutes and the potatoes after 20 to 30 minutes; each should be tender when pierced but still hold its shape. Drain promptly so the vegetables do not become waterlogged.

instructions.name: Blanch and dry the peas
instructions.text: Bring 2 cups water to a boil in a small saucepan. Add the frozen peas and cook for 60 seconds, just until hot and bright green. Drain in a fine-mesh sieve, rinse briefly under cold water and spread on a clean towel to dry.

instructions.name: Cool before cutting
instructions.text: Spread the cooked beets, potatoes and carrots on separate plates or a rimmed sheet pan. Cool at room temperature for no more than 1 hour, then refrigerate uncovered for 30 to 45 minutes, until cool and firm. Do not seal warm vegetables in a container; trapped steam makes the potatoes crumbly and the salad watery.

instructions.name: Make a sharp sunflower dressing
instructions.text: Whisk 2 tablespoons sunflower oil with the pickle brine, Dijon, remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt and black pepper in a large bowl. Add the pickles, sauerkraut, onion, peas and chopped dill, tossing so the briny ingredients are evenly distributed.

instructions.name: Cut uniform 3/8-inch dice
instructions.text: Peel the potatoes only if their skins are tough. Cut the cooled potatoes and carrots into 3/8-inch dice. Cut the beets last, using a washable board, so their color does not transfer to every vegetable before mixing.

instructions.name: Oil the beets before folding
instructions.text: Place the diced beets in a separate bowl and toss with the remaining 1 tablespoon oil. Fold the potatoes and carrots into the dressed pickle mixture, then fold in the oiled beets with 6 to 8 broad strokes. Stop while the vegetables remain visibly distinct rather than stirring until everything turns uniformly magenta.

instructions.name: Rest, taste and serve cool
instructions.text: Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes or up to 24 hours. Taste cold and adjust with salt, pepper or pickle brine 1 teaspoon at a time. Serve cool, not ice-cold, with extra dill or parsley. Refrigerate the salad within 2 hours of assembly.

why_it_works: Cooking beets separately prevents their long simmer and strong pigment from overcooking or prematurely staining the potatoes and carrots.
Cooling the root vegetables before cutting firms their starch and pectin, which produces tidy dice instead of ragged, mashed edges.
Squeezing the sauerkraut and drying the peas removes excess liquid, so the dressing stays bright rather than pooling at the bottom of the bowl.
Coating the beets with oil before the final fold slows color transfer and preserves the salad's visible red, gold, orange and green components.
Pickle brine, mustard and fermented cabbage add enough acidity to balance the sweet roots without covering their flavor with a heavy mayonnaise dressing.
swaps: Use canned beets only when time matters more than texture: drain very well, pat dry and add them at the final fold. Avoid sweet pickled beets, which unbalance the savory dressing.
Replace the peas with 1 cup drained, rinsed white beans for a more substantial lunch salad. Dry the beans well and fold them in with the potatoes.
If sauerkraut is unavailable, increase the dill pickles to 1 1/2 cups and add 2 teaspoons extra pickle brine; the flavor will be less fermented but still balanced.
Yellow onion or thinly sliced scallions can replace red onion. Soak a sharp yellow onion in cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and dry before mixing.
Unrefined sunflower oil gives the most characteristic nutty aroma, but a mild extra-virgin olive oil or neutral grapeseed oil works without changing the method.
storage: Refrigerate vinegret in a shallow airtight container within 2 hours and use within 4 days. The flavor improves overnight, although the colors become more uniform. Do not freeze it: thawed potatoes and pickles turn mealy and watery. Serve leftovers cool or let a portion stand for 15 minutes; reheating destroys the crisp pickle contrast. If liquid collects, drain it off and refresh each 4-cup portion with 1 teaspoon pickle brine and 1 teaspoon sunflower oil.
notes: Cultural context and sourcing: vinegret is shared across several Eastern European and post-Soviet food traditions. This Ukrainian-style version follows the beet, potato, carrot, pickle, sauerkraut and sunflower-oil pattern documented by current Ukrainian community and cookery sources, including UAFest's 2026 vinehret recipe and Yevhen Klopotenko's Ukrainian recipe archive; the label describes this preparation rather than claiming exclusive origin.

Photo-match record: the licensed photograph clearly shows a finished bowl of diced beet salad with recognizable potato, carrot and green peas. Those visible major components, ruby color, small dice and bowl presentation all match this recipe; the alt text does not claim that supporting pickles or sauerkraut are individually visible.

Vegetable cooking-and-cooling matrix — beets: simmer whole 40 to 60 minutes, then skin and chill; carrots: simmer whole 15 to 20 minutes, then drain and chill; Yukon Gold potatoes: simmer whole 20 to 30 minutes, then drain and chill; peas: blanch 60 seconds, rinse and dry. Remove each item when a knife enters with light resistance rather than waiting for one shared timer.

Uniform-dice guide: aim for 3/8-inch cubes, roughly the size of a green pea. Larger pieces taste disconnected; smaller pieces collapse during folding. Cut potatoes first, carrots second and beets last, wiping the knife and board after the beets.

Make-ahead texture rescue — watery bowl: drain and add 1 teaspoon oil; bland after chilling: add pickle brine 1 teaspoon at a time; overly sour: fold in 1/2 cup extra cooked potato; fully pink but intact: serve as-is because the flavor is unaffected; crumbling potato: stop stirring and use a flexible spatula for the final folds.

Two-day schedule: cook and chill the roots up to 2 days ahead in separate covered containers; dice and assemble up to 24 hours ahead; reserve a spoonful of herbs and peas to scatter on top immediately before serving for fresh contrast.

faqs.q: How do I keep vinegret from turning completely pink?
faqs.a: Cool every vegetable fully, cut the beets last and toss them with 1 tablespoon oil before the final fold. Mix with a flexible spatula using only 6 to 8 broad strokes. Some color migration is traditional and inevitable by the next day, but this sequence keeps the components distinct when first served.

faqs.q: Can I roast the beets instead of boiling them?
faqs.a: Yes. Wrap scrubbed beets together in foil, place on a rimmed pan and roast at 400°F for 50 to 75 minutes, until a knife enters easily. Cool before peeling. Roasting concentrates sweetness and avoids a red-stained pot, but the beets may be slightly drier, so taste the finished salad and add 1 teaspoon extra brine if needed.

faqs.q: Is Ukrainian vinegret served warm or cold?
faqs.a: It is usually served cool or at room temperature, after the dressing has had time to season the vegetables. Chill the assembled salad for at least 30 minutes, then let the serving bowl stand for about 15 minutes so the sunflower oil loosens and the flavors are easier to taste. Keep the total time out of refrigeration under 2 hours.
